newsitem.title: USA: Clinton gains backing for student testing plan.
newsitem.headline: Clinton gains backing for student testing plan.

text.p: President Clinton won support on Friday from 15 of the nation's largest school districts for his call for voluntary performance tests for math and reading and chided most states for not joining them.

"Beginning with our nation's elementary schools, we have to demand excellence from every school, every teacher, every student," Clinton said in a speech to a convention of the National Association of Elementary School Principals.
"We have to repair and rebuild our schools," he said, calling for new technologies in the classroom and a drug free environment for the nation's school children.

"I believe that the single most important thing that we can do to give our children world class education is to insist on high national standards so that we make sure that we have done everything that we can to see that every single child learns...to succeed in the exciting world of the 21st Century," he said.
Clinton has made upgrading the quality of education across the United States a key goal of his second term and has pushed for national standards and testing for elementary school children.

He announced that 15 school districts -- including New York, Los Angeles and Chicago, the nation's three largest -- agreed to participate in his plan for voluntary national tests in fourth grade reading and eighth grade math by 1999.
"For too long we have been unwilling to insist upon that as a nation, perhaps for fear that some of our children could not reach those standards," Clinton declared.

Noting that he would be in Las Vegas on Monday to address a National Governors Association meeting, Clinton said that most governors had been slow to embrace his call for voluntary testing. Only seven have endorsed the idea.
"They've been dragging their feet," Clinton complained, saying that in past years "the governors would have been the first group out there" promoting the plan.

In addition to the biggest three, school districts to endorse his programme included: Philadelphia, Atlanta, Broward County, Fla., Cincinnati, Detroit, Houston, San Antonio, El Paso, Omaha, Long Beach, Fresno and Seattle.

"This commitment means that three and a half million more children, one out of every 14 public school children in America, will be held to these world-class education standards and the basics," Clinton said.

"And it means after the test is given, all of them will get a better education because we'll all learn from the test results and keep working until we get the results we want in every one of those districts," he said.
Thus far, seven states have said they will participate in Clinton's programme -- Kentucky, Maryland, Michigan, North Carolina, California, Massachusetts and West Virginia.
Clinton hailed recently released test results that for the first time in decades found American school children performing above the international average in both math and science.
The test scores show that "we don't have to settle for second-class expectations, or second-class goals for any of our children," Clinton said.

In the math scores, where traditional American youngsters have trailed far behind their foreign counterparts, the average score was above the international norm. Only students in Japan, South Korea, Singapore, the Netherlands, the Czech Republic and Austria performed better.
